title: Assertions and Defensive Programming
learning_outcomes: Explain the central rule or purpose of assertions and defensive programming using at least one correct term from the lesson.
Interpret or adapt a small Kotlin example that demonstrates assertions and defensive programming.
Identify one relevant edge case, debugging step, or version/platform constraint.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn **Assertions and Defensive Programming** as part of **Testing, Debugging, Documentation, and Quality**. Reliable Kotlin code is supported by repeatable tests, meaningful assertions, debuggable failure reports, documentation, and review—not by coverage alone. Use the subtopics—Preconditions and Postconditions, The require and check Functions, Invariants and Defensive Validation—as a checklist: predict what the example will do, then verify it in a project configured for the target platform.
content.why_it_matters: Professional applications need repeatable tests, clear APIs, dependable dependencies, security checks, and observable failures. Apply this concept in small steps before integrating it into a larger project.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Reliable Kotlin code is supported by repeatable tests, meaningful assertions, debuggable failure reports, documentation, and review—not by coverage alone.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with preconditions and postconditions. Then compare it with the require and check functions. Identify the input, state, dependency, or branch that determines the result. The snippet is a static reference for CodeLeaf and is not executed in the lesson page.

items.title: Preconditions and Postconditions
items.text: Preconditions and Postconditions is one part of assertions and defensive programming. Connect its definition to the example, identify the input/state it changes, and verify the expected behavior with a small test case.

items.title: The require and check Functions
items.text: The require and check Functions describes how behavior is declared, passed, or composed. Make inputs and return types clear, keep side effects visible, and use a small call-site example to judge readability.

items.title: Invariants and Defensive Validation
items.text: Invariants and Defensive Validation defines a trust boundary. Validate untrusted input at the boundary, keep secrets server-side, check authorization where the protected operation occurs, and test both allowed and rejected cases.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Assertions and Defensive Programming removes the need to test boundary conditions or verify the chosen runtime/library version.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the example fails, first confirm which runtime/project type the snippet requires. Read the first useful compiler or runtime message, check imports and declared dependencies, reduce the example to a minimal case, and rerun. For target-specific code, use the target toolchain rather than assuming a console or browser runner can execute it.
